title: Act II, Scene IV

teacherSummary.text: Ross and an Old Man describe unnatural events: darkness by day, a falcon killed by a 'mousing owl', and Duncan's horses breaking loose and eating each other. Macduff reports that the princes are suspected of bribing the grooms, that Macbeth has been named king and has gone to Scone to be invested, and that Duncan's body has been carried to Colmekill. Macduff will not go to Scone but home to Fife.

context.history: The idea of a 'great chain of being' held that a king's murder disordered nature; Holinshed's chronicle supplied the omens of the horses and the darkness.

significance: The omens turn the murder into a cosmic crime. Macduff's quiet refusal to attend the coronation is the first sign of resistance.
discussionQuestions: Do you think the natural world reflects human events? Why do stories so often say it does?

segments.script: The idea of a 'great chain of being' held that a king's murder disordered nature; Holinshed's chronicle supplied the omens of the horses and the darkness. The omens turn the murder into a cosmic crime. Macduff's quiet refusal to attend the coronation is the first sign of resistance. Setting: An Old Man and Ross describe unnatural events: darkness by day, a falcon killed by an owl, Duncan's horses eating each other. Imagery: Nature in revolt mirrors the moral disorder. Characterization: Macduff refuses to attend the coronation at Scone: the first sign of resistance. Watch for kingship and order: Rightful kingship (Duncan, Edward, Malcolm) is tied to natural order; tyranny to disorder. In this scene: “They were suborn’d: / Malcolm and Donalbain, the king’s two sons, / Are stol’n away and fled; which puts upon them” (Act II, Scene IV, Macduff).

segments.activity: Model the close reading of the anchor quotation using the written think-aloud below.
segments.script: First, meaning. I read “by the clock, ’tis day, / And yet dark night strangles the travelling lamp” slowly and put it in my own words: Ross says that by the clock it is day, yet dark night strangles the sun. Next, craft. I notice the violent verb "strangles," applied to night killing daylight. The strongest word is “strangles”: it makes the darkness a murderer, echoing Duncan's death. Then, effect. What does Ross notice about the unnatural darkness? My answer: Ross notices that the unnatural darkness covers the day after the king's murder; nature itself seems disordered, which shows that the crime has upset the whole order of the world.

segments.script: Annotate the scene for setting, imagery (three marks with a margin note each), then write one claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph: what does this scene suggest about nature's revolt against the crime? Then start your writing prompt at your assigned level (HS Sophomore: Analyze how Act II, Scene IV develops the idea of nature's revolt against the crime. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of imagery and symbolism shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.) Exemplar: The unnatural events after Duncan's murder show that the crime has disturbed the order of the universe. When the text says “by the clock, ’tis day, / And yet dark night strangles the travelling lamp” (Act II, Scene IV, Ross), it shows this directly. Ross sees that "dark night strangles the travelling lamp" by day, and a falcon is killed by "a mousing owl," a lower creature overthrowing a higher, just as Macbeth killed his king.
